notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Climate refers to the long-term average pattern of weather conditions over a large area.
  • It includes temperature, atmospheric pressure, winds, humidity and precipitation.
  • Weather refers to short-term atmospheric conditions at a particular place and time.
  • Climate is relatively stable over long periods, while weather changes frequently.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Weather → Short-term atmospheric condition

Climate → Long-term average condition

2. India's Climate
  • India has a monsoon-type climate.
  • The most important feature is the seasonal reversal of winds.
  • India's climate shows considerable regional variation because of its large size and varied relief.
  • Temperature, rainfall and season length differ greatly from one part of India to another.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → Tropical Monsoon Climate

3. Meaning of Monsoon
  • The word monsoon is derived from the Arabic word mausim, meaning season.
  • Monsoon refers to the seasonal reversal of wind direction.
  • India's rainfall regime is closely linked with this seasonal wind reversal.
4. Major Controls of India's Climate

The major climatic controls are:

  • Latitude.
  • Altitude.
  • Distance from the sea.
  • Relief.
  • Pressure and wind systems.
  • Himalayan Mountains.
  • Western Ghats.
  • Jet streams.
  • Ocean-atmosphere interactions.
5. Latitude
  • Tropic of Cancer passes through central India.
  • Areas south of it lie mainly in tropical latitudes.
  • Areas north of it lie mainly in subtropical latitudes.
  • Therefore, southern India generally experiences smaller seasonal temperature variations than northern India.
6. Tropic of Cancer
  • Tropic of Cancer lies at 23°30′ N.
  • It divides India approximately into tropical and subtropical zones.
  • It crosses eight Indian states.
7. Altitude
  • Temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude.
  • Mountain regions are cooler than nearby plains.
  • Himalayan hill stations can remain cool even when adjoining plains are very hot.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Altitude ↑ → Temperature ↓

8. Normal Lapse Rate
  • Air temperature generally decreases with altitude in the lower atmosphere.
  • A commonly cited average environmental lapse rate is about 6.5°C per 1,000 metres.
  • Actual lapse rates vary with atmospheric conditions.
9. Distance from Sea
  • Coastal areas experience maritime influence.
  • Oceans heat and cool slowly.
  • Therefore, coastal regions have smaller annual temperature ranges.
  • Interior areas experience greater temperature extremes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Coastal Climate → Equable

Interior Climate → Continental

10. Continentality
  • Continentality refers to climatic effects of distance from the sea.
  • Inland areas heat strongly during summer and cool more during winter.
  • Delhi shows stronger seasonal temperature variation than Chennai or Mumbai.
11. Maritime Influence
  • Coastal cities have relatively moderate temperatures.
  • Chennai, Mumbai and Kochi show less annual temperature variation than inland northern cities.
  • Humidity is generally higher near the coast.
12. Himalayas and Climate
  • The Himalayas block extremely cold continental winds from Central Asia.
  • They prevent monsoon winds from escaping freely northward.
  • They force moisture-bearing winds to rise and produce rainfall.
  • They therefore play a major role in India's monsoon climate.
📌 Must-Memorise

Himalayas → Climatic Barrier

13. Western Ghats and Climate
  • Western Ghats form an important orographic barrier.
  • Arabian Sea monsoon winds rise along their western slopes.
  • Heavy rainfall occurs on the windward side.
  • Interior Deccan lies partly in the rain shadow.
14. Orographic Rainfall
  • Orographic rainfall occurs when moist air is forced to rise over mountains.
  • Rising air cools and condenses.
  • Windward slopes receive higher rainfall.
  • Leeward slopes generally receive less rainfall.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Western Ghats → Orographic Rainfall

15. Rain Shadow
  • A rain-shadow region lies on the leeward side of a mountain barrier.
  • Descending air becomes relatively warmer and drier.
  • Parts of interior Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu are influenced by the Western Ghats rain shadow during the southwest monsoon.
16. Pressure and Wind Systems

India's seasonal climate depends strongly on:

  • Changing land and sea temperatures.
  • Seasonal pressure differences.
  • Movement of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone.
  • Upper-air circulation.
  • Monsoon winds.
17. Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone
  • ITCZ is a low-pressure zone near the Equator where trade winds converge.
  • It shifts north and south seasonally with the apparent movement of the Sun.
  • Its northward movement during northern summer influences the Indian monsoon.
📌 Must-Memorise

ITCZ → Low Pressure + Converging Trade Winds

18. Monsoon Trough
  • During summer, the ITCZ shifts northward over the Indian subcontinent.
  • This elongated low-pressure zone is often called the monsoon trough.
  • Its position strongly affects rainfall distribution.
19. Heating of Indian Landmass
  • During summer, the Indian landmass heats rapidly.
  • Low atmospheric pressure develops over northwestern India and adjoining regions.
  • The Indian Ocean remains relatively cooler and has higher pressure.
  • This pressure contrast encourages moisture-bearing winds to move toward India.
20. Tibetan Plateau
  • The Tibetan Plateau becomes intensely heated during summer.
  • It contributes to large-scale atmospheric circulation changes over Asia.
  • Its elevated heating helps strengthen the summer monsoon circulation.
21. Winter Pressure Conditions
  • During winter, the Indian landmass cools.
  • High pressure develops over northern and central India.
  • Winds generally move from land toward surrounding seas.
  • Most of India therefore experiences dry winter conditions.
22. Coriolis Force
  • Earth's rotation deflects moving air.
  • In the Northern Hemisphere, winds are deflected to the right.
  • This deflection influences monsoon wind direction.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Northern Hemisphere → Deflection to Right

23. Southeast Trade Winds
  • Southeast trade winds originate over the southern Indian Ocean.
  • They cross the Equator during northern summer.
  • After crossing the Equator, Coriolis deflection turns them toward the southwest.
  • They reach India as the southwest monsoon.
📌 Must-Memorise

SE Trade Winds Cross Equator → SW Monsoon

24. Cross-Equatorial Flow
  • Cross-equatorial flow is a major feature of the southwest monsoon.
  • Winds from the southern Indian Ocean move across the Equator toward low pressure over South Asia.
  • They acquire large quantities of moisture over the ocean.
25. Mascarene High
  • A strong subtropical high-pressure region develops over the southern Indian Ocean near the Mascarene Islands.
  • It contributes to cross-equatorial monsoon flow toward India.
  • Strong pressure gradients can support stronger monsoon winds.
26. Somali Jet
  • A strong low-level cross-equatorial wind current develops near the east coast of Africa during northern summer.
  • It is commonly called the Somali Jet.
  • It helps transport moisture toward the Arabian Sea branch of the Indian monsoon.
27. Jet Streams
  • Jet streams are narrow bands of very strong winds in the upper atmosphere.
  • Their seasonal positions influence the Indian monsoon.
  • Two important concepts are:
  • Subtropical Westerly Jet.
  • Tropical Easterly Jet.
28. Subtropical Westerly Jet
  • During winter, a subtropical westerly jet flows south of the Himalayas.
  • It influences winter weather over northern India.
  • Its northward shift during summer is associated with monsoon development.
29. Tropical Easterly Jet
  • During summer, an upper-air easterly jet develops over peninsular India and adjoining regions.
  • It is associated with the southwest monsoon circulation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Winter → Westerly Jet

Summer → Tropical Easterly Jet

30. Seasonal Classification of India

India's climate is commonly divided into four seasons:

  • Cold Weather Season.
  • Hot Weather Season.
  • Southwest Monsoon Season.
  • Retreating or Northeast Monsoon Season.
31. Cold Weather Season
  • Cold weather season generally extends from December to February.
  • January is usually the coldest month over much of northern India.
  • Temperatures decrease from south to north.
  • Northern plains experience cool days and cold nights.
  • Peninsular India remains comparatively warm.
32. Winter Temperature Pattern
  • Northern India can experience temperatures near freezing in some inland areas.
  • Southern coastal regions remain much warmer.
  • Peninsular temperatures are moderated by the sea.
33. Winter Pressure Pattern
  • High pressure develops over northern India.
  • Surface winds generally blow from land toward sea.
  • These winds are mainly dry because they originate over the continent.
34. Winter Winds
  • Winter surface winds generally blow from northeast toward southwest.
  • They are called northeast trade-like winds in textbook descriptions.
  • Most of India remains dry.
35. Tamil Nadu Winter Rainfall Exception
  • Northeast winds cross the Bay of Bengal before reaching Tamil Nadu.
  • They pick up moisture.
  • Therefore, Tamil Nadu receives important rainfall during the retreating/northeast monsoon season.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu → Major Rainfall from Northeast Monsoon

36. Western Disturbances
  • Western disturbances are eastward-moving extratropical weather systems.
  • They originate broadly in the Mediterranean-West Asian region.
  • They travel eastward with the westerlies.
  • They bring winter rainfall to northwestern India and snowfall to the western Himalayas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Western Disturbances → Winter Rain in NW India

37. Importance of Western Disturbances

Winter rainfall from western disturbances benefits:

  • Wheat.
  • Mustard.
  • Other rabi crops.

Snowfall also contributes to Himalayan snowpack.

38. Mahawat
  • Winter rainfall in northwestern India is sometimes traditionally called mahawat.
  • It is valuable for rabi crops.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mahawat → Winter Rainfall → Rabi Crops

39. Hot Weather Season
  • Hot weather season generally extends from March to May.
  • Temperatures rise rapidly as the Sun moves northward.
  • May is often among the hottest months over northwestern India.
  • Low pressure strengthens over northern and northwestern India.
40. Summer Temperature Pattern
  • Northwestern and interior regions become extremely hot.
  • Coastal areas remain relatively moderate.
  • Peninsular highlands remain cooler than surrounding lowlands.
41. Loo
  • Loo is a hot, dry and often strong wind.
  • It blows over the northern and northwestern plains during summer afternoons.
  • It is especially common in Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh.
📌 Must-Memorise

Loo → Hot, Dry Summer Wind of North India

42. Heat Waves
  • Heat waves occur when unusually high temperatures persist over an area.
  • Northwestern, central and eastern interior India can experience severe heat waves.
  • Dry soil and clear skies can intensify extreme temperatures.
43. Dust Storms
  • Dust storms are common in northwestern India during the hot season.
  • Strong winds lift loose dry soil and dust.
  • They may temporarily reduce temperature after passage.
44. Local Summer Thunderstorms

Pre-monsoon thunderstorms occur in several regions under local names.

Important examples:

  • Kalbaisakhi.
  • Nor'westers.
  • Mango showers.
  • Blossom showers.
45. Kalbaisakhi
  • Kalbaisakhi are violent pre-monsoon thunderstorms in West Bengal and adjoining eastern India.
  • They are also called Nor'westers.
  • They occur mainly during April and May.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kalbaisakhi → Bengal → Pre-Monsoon Thunderstorm

46. Nor'westers
  • Nor'westers affect West Bengal, Assam and adjoining northeastern/eastern regions.
  • They can bring strong winds, lightning and heavy rain.
  • They are useful for some crops but can cause damage.
47. Mango Showers
  • Pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and Karnataka are commonly called mango showers.
  • They help the early ripening of mangoes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mango Showers → Kerala and Karnataka

48. Blossom Showers
  • Pre-monsoon showers in coffee-growing areas of Karnataka are often called blossom showers.
  • They help stimulate coffee flowering.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Blossom Showers → Coffee

49. Southwest Monsoon Season
  • Southwest monsoon season generally extends from June to September.
  • It provides the majority of India's annual rainfall.
  • Moist winds arrive from the Indian Ocean.
  • Rainfall varies greatly across India.
50. Onset of Southwest Monsoon
  • The southwest monsoon usually reaches Kerala around the beginning of June.
  • Its arrival is marked by a sudden increase in rainfall.
  • This rapid change is often called the burst of the monsoon.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

SW Monsoon First Major Landfall → Kerala

51. Burst of Monsoon
  • The onset often produces a dramatic increase in rainfall.
  • Winds strengthen.
  • Humidity rises.
  • Cloudiness increases.
  • Temperatures may fall.
52. Advance of Monsoon
  • After reaching Kerala, the monsoon advances northward and northwestward.
  • It usually covers most of India over several weeks.
  • The exact dates vary from year to year.
53. Two Branches of Southwest Monsoon

The southwest monsoon is traditionally divided into:

  • Arabian Sea Branch.
  • Bay of Bengal Branch.
📌 Must-Memorise

SW Monsoon → Arabian Sea + Bay of Bengal Branches

54. Arabian Sea Branch
  • The Arabian Sea branch strikes the Western Ghats.
  • Heavy rainfall occurs along the west coast and windward slopes.
  • The branch then moves inland.
55. Western Ghats Rainfall
  • Moist winds rise sharply over the Western Ghats.
  • Konkan, coastal Karnataka and Kerala receive heavy rainfall.
  • The leeward Deccan Plateau receives much less rainfall.
56. Rain Shadow of Western Ghats

Important rain-shadow areas occur in parts of:

  • Interior Maharashtra.
  • Karnataka.
  • Telangana.
  • Western/interior Tamil Nadu.
57. Arabian Sea Branch and Northern India
  • One part of the Arabian Sea branch moves northward toward Gujarat and Rajasthan.
  • Another contributes rainfall farther inland over central and northern India.
58. Bay of Bengal Branch
  • The Bay of Bengal branch moves toward northeastern India.
  • Moist air is channelled toward the Ganga-Brahmaputra region.
  • Relief causes extremely heavy rainfall in parts of Meghalaya and northeastern India.
59. Meghalaya Orographic Rainfall
  • Moist Bay of Bengal winds enter the Bengal-Assam region.
  • They encounter the steep southern slopes of the Meghalaya Plateau.
  • Rapid uplift produces exceptionally heavy rainfall.
60. Mawsynram
  • Mawsynram lies in Meghalaya.
  • It is famous for extremely high average annual rainfall.
  • Its position on the southern Khasi Hills produces strong orographic uplift.
📌 Must-Memorise

Very Heavy Rainfall → Mawsynram → Meghalaya

61. Cherrapunji
  • Cherrapunji, also called Sohra, lies in Meghalaya.
  • It is another exceptionally wet location.
  • It lies close to Mawsynram in the Khasi Hills.
62. Khasi Hills and Rainfall
  • The southern Khasi escarpment faces moisture-bearing Bay of Bengal winds.
  • Funnel-shaped relief enhances uplift.
  • Heavy orographic rainfall results.
63. Bay Branch Along Ganga Plain
  • After reaching northeastern India, part of the Bay of Bengal branch turns westward.
  • It moves along the Ganga Plain.
  • Rainfall generally decreases from east to west across the northern plains.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Northern Plain Monsoon Rain → Generally Decreases East to West

64. Why Rainfall Decreases Westward
  • Monsoon winds progressively lose moisture as they travel inland.
  • Therefore, eastern parts of the Ganga Plain receive more rainfall than western parts.
65. Monsoon Trough and Rainfall
  • The monsoon trough shifts north and south during the rainy season.
  • Its position influences areas of concentrated rainfall.
  • North-south movement causes wet and dry spells.
66. Break in the Monsoon
  • A break in monsoon means a temporary reduction or interruption of rainfall over large parts of the monsoon zone.
  • It can last for several days.
  • Rainfall may remain concentrated near the Himalayan foothills or other regions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Monsoon Break → Temporary Dry Spell

67. Active Monsoon
  • During active monsoon conditions, widespread rainfall occurs over large parts of India.
  • Low-pressure systems and favourable monsoon trough positions often strengthen rainfall.
68. Monsoon Depressions
  • Low-pressure systems frequently form over the Bay of Bengal during the monsoon.
  • They move westward or northwestward across India.
  • They distribute rainfall deep into the interior.
69. Importance of Bay Depressions
  • Central India receives much of its monsoon rainfall from depressions and low-pressure systems originating over the Bay of Bengal.
  • Their tracks strongly influence seasonal rainfall distribution.
70. Variability of Monsoon

Monsoon rainfall varies:

  • From year to year.
  • From region to region.
  • Within the same season.
  • In onset and withdrawal dates.

This variability has major agricultural consequences.

71. Uneven Distribution of Rainfall

India contains:

  • Extremely wet regions.
  • Moderate-rainfall regions.
  • Semi-arid regions.
  • Deserts.

This variation results from relief, wind direction, distance from sea and monsoon circulation.

72. High-Rainfall Regions

Areas receiving high rainfall include:

  • Western slopes of Western Ghats.
  • Meghalaya.
  • Assam.
  • Parts of Arunachal Pradesh.
  • Some Himalayan foothills.
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
73. Low-Rainfall Regions

Low rainfall occurs in:

  • Western Rajasthan.
  • Ladakh.
  • Interior rain-shadow regions of the Deccan.
  • Some parts of western Tamil Nadu during the southwest monsoon.
74. Ladakh — Low Rainfall
  • Ladakh lies in the rain shadow of the Himalayas.
  • Moist monsoon winds are largely blocked before reaching it.
  • It therefore has a cold-desert climate.
75. Rajasthan — Low Rainfall
  • Rajasthan lies far inland.
  • Arabian Sea monsoon winds travel roughly parallel to much of the Aravalli.
  • Moisture decreases inland.
  • Therefore, western Rajasthan receives low rainfall.
76. Retreating Monsoon Season
  • Retreating monsoon season generally occurs during October and November.
  • The southwest monsoon gradually withdraws from northern India.
  • Atmospheric pressure patterns reverse.
  • Winds begin to blow from land toward the sea.
77. Monsoon Withdrawal
  • Withdrawal generally begins from northwestern India.
  • It progresses southward and eastward.
  • Skies become clearer.
  • Temperatures can remain high while humidity remains substantial.
78. October Heat
  • October heat refers to hot and humid conditions during the retreating monsoon period.
  • High humidity makes temperatures feel uncomfortable.
  • It is especially noticeable in northern and central parts shortly after the rainy season.
📌 Must-Memorise

October Heat → Hot + Humid Retreating Monsoon Condition

79. Northeast Monsoon
  • During October-December, winds over southern India increasingly blow from the northeast.
  • These winds cross the Bay of Bengal before reaching southeastern India.
  • They acquire moisture and bring rainfall to Tamil Nadu and adjoining regions.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

NE Monsoon → October–December → Tamil Nadu

80. Tamil Nadu Rainfall Pattern
  • Tamil Nadu lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats during much of the southwest monsoon.
  • Therefore, it receives a smaller proportion of rainfall from the southwest monsoon compared with India's western coast.
  • A major share of Tamil Nadu's annual rainfall occurs during the northeast monsoon.
81. Why Tamil Nadu Gets Winter/Retreating Rain
  • Northeast winds begin as continental winds.
  • They cross the Bay of Bengal.
  • They absorb moisture.
  • They then strike the Coromandel Coast.
  • Cyclonic depressions further enhance rainfall.
82. Coromandel Coast Rainfall
  • Coromandel Coast receives significant rainfall during October-November and extending into December.
  • This contrasts sharply with most of India, where these months mark the end of the main rainy season.
83. Cyclonic Rainfall in Tamil Nadu
  • Bay of Bengal cyclones and depressions frequently affect Tamil Nadu during the northeast monsoon season.
  • They can produce very heavy rainfall.
  • Coastal districts are particularly vulnerable.
84. Northeast Monsoon Importance to Agriculture

The northeast monsoon is vital for:

  • Reservoir recharge.
  • Tank irrigation.
  • Paddy cultivation.
  • Groundwater recharge.
  • Drinking-water supply in Tamil Nadu.
85. Tamil Nadu and Southwest Monsoon
  • Western Tamil Nadu receives some southwest monsoon rainfall where topography permits.
  • Nilgiris and western slopes receive substantial rainfall.
  • Eastern and southeastern Tamil Nadu receive relatively less from this monsoon.
86. Nilgiris Rainfall
  • Nilgiris receive rainfall from both monsoon systems to varying degrees.
  • Western-facing slopes receive southwest monsoon rain.
  • Seasonal circulation and local relief create complex rainfall patterns.
87. Kanyakumari Rainfall
  • Kanyakumari's southern location allows influence from both southwest and northeast monsoons.
  • Relief also modifies local rainfall.
88. Annual Rainfall Distribution

India's rainfall pattern is highly uneven.

Broadly:

  • Very high rainfall → Western Ghats and northeast.
  • Moderate rainfall → Ganga Plain and central India.
  • Low rainfall → Interior Deccan and northwestern India.
  • Very low rainfall → Western Rajasthan and Ladakh.
89. Rainfall Isohyet
  • An isohyet is a line joining places receiving equal rainfall.
📌 Must-Memorise

Isohyet → Equal Rainfall

90. Isotherm
  • An isotherm is a line joining places with equal temperature.
📌 Must-Memorise

Isotherm → Equal Temperature

91. Isobar
  • An isobar is a line joining places with equal atmospheric pressure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Isobar → Equal Pressure

92. Humidity
  • Humidity refers to water vapour present in air.
  • Coastal regions generally have high humidity.
  • Dry inland areas have lower humidity, especially before monsoon arrival.
93. Relative Humidity
  • Relative humidity is the amount of water vapour present relative to the maximum amount air can hold at that temperature.
  • It is expressed as a percentage.
94. Temperature Range
  • Temperature range means difference between maximum and minimum temperatures over a specified period.
  • Coastal regions have smaller temperature ranges.
  • Inland northwestern regions have larger ranges.
95. Diurnal Temperature Range
  • Diurnal range is the difference between daytime maximum and nighttime minimum temperatures.
  • Deserts often show large diurnal ranges.
96. Annual Temperature Range
  • Annual range is the difference between mean temperatures of the warmest and coldest months.
  • Northern interior India shows larger annual ranges than southern coastal India.
97. Chennai Climate
  • Chennai has a tropical coastal climate.
  • The Bay of Bengal moderates temperature.
  • Humidity is often high.
  • Northeast monsoon contributes a major share of annual rainfall.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Chennai → Coastal + NE Monsoon Dominance

98. Mumbai Climate
  • Mumbai has a maritime tropical climate.
  • Annual temperature range is relatively small.
  • Southwest monsoon rainfall is heavy.
  • Humidity is high.
99. Delhi Climate
  • Delhi has a more continental climate.
  • Summers are very hot.
  • Winters are cool to cold.
  • Annual temperature range is much greater than in Mumbai or Chennai.
100. Kolkata Climate
  • Kolkata has a humid subtropical/tropical monsoon-influenced climate.
  • It receives heavy southwest monsoon rainfall.
  • Summers are hot and humid.
101. Bengaluru Climate
  • Bengaluru lies at a relatively high elevation on the Deccan Plateau.
  • Its elevation moderates temperatures.
  • It is cooler than many nearby lowland locations at similar latitudes.
102. Hill-Station Climate
  • Higher altitude lowers temperature.
  • Ooty, Kodaikanal, Shimla and similar locations remain cooler than surrounding plains.
  • Relief and exposure influence rainfall.
103. India's Climatic Unity

Despite regional variation, India's climate has a common monsoon rhythm:

  • Summer heating.
  • Monsoon onset.
  • Rainy season.
  • Monsoon withdrawal.
  • Winter dry season in most regions.
104. India's Climatic Diversity

Examples include:

  • Hot desert climate of western Rajasthan.
  • Cold desert of Ladakh.
  • Humid climate of northeast India.
  • Equable coastal climates.
  • Cool mountain climates.
  • Semi-arid interior plateau climate.
105. Monsoon and Agriculture
  • Indian agriculture remains strongly influenced by monsoon rainfall.
  • Rainfall determines sowing conditions for many kharif crops.
  • Weak or delayed monsoon can cause drought.
  • Excess monsoon rainfall can cause floods.
106. Kharif Crops
  • Kharif crops are generally sown with the onset of the southwest monsoon.
  • Rice, maize, cotton, soybean and groundnut are important examples.
  • Exact cropping seasons vary by region.
107. Rabi Crops
  • Rabi crops are generally sown after the monsoon and grown during cooler months.
  • Wheat, mustard and gram are important examples.
  • Winter rainfall from western disturbances can benefit northwestern rabi crops.
108. Monsoon and Water Resources
  • Reservoirs depend heavily on seasonal rainfall.
  • Groundwater recharge is strongly influenced by monsoon precipitation.
  • Rivers, tanks and lakes are replenished during rainy periods.
109. Monsoon and Hydroelectricity
  • Rainfall increases reservoir storage.
  • Hydropower generation depends on water availability.
  • Weak monsoon years can reduce hydropower generation.
110. Monsoon and Economy

The monsoon affects:

  • Agriculture.
  • Food production.
  • Rural income.
  • Hydropower.
  • Water supply.
  • Inflation.
  • Transport.
  • Disaster risk.
111. Drought
  • Drought is a prolonged period of abnormally low water availability.
  • Meteorological drought involves deficient rainfall.
  • Agricultural drought involves inadequate soil moisture for crops.
  • Hydrological drought involves reduced river, reservoir and groundwater levels.
112. Meteorological Drought
  • Meteorological drought is based primarily on rainfall deficiency compared with normal conditions.
113. Agricultural Drought
  • Agricultural drought occurs when soil moisture becomes insufficient for crops.
  • It can develop even when total seasonal rainfall is not extremely low if rainfall distribution is poor.
114. Hydrological Drought
  • Hydrological drought affects rivers, reservoirs, lakes and groundwater.
  • It often develops after prolonged rainfall deficiency.
115. Floods
  • Excessive monsoon rainfall can cause floods.
  • Himalayan rivers, Brahmaputra Valley and Ganga plains are especially flood-prone.
  • Cyclonic rainfall can cause severe coastal flooding.
116. Cloudburst
  • A cloudburst is an extremely intense rainfall event over a small area in a short period.
  • It is especially dangerous in mountainous regions.
  • Flash floods and landslides may result.
117. Flash Flood
  • Flash floods develop rapidly after intense rainfall, cloudbursts or sudden release of water.
  • Mountain valleys and urban areas with poor drainage are vulnerable.
118. El Niño
  • El Niño is abnormal warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean.
  • It alters atmospheric circulation across the tropics.
  • Many El Niño years have been associated with weaker Indian monsoon rainfall, but the relationship is not absolute.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

El Niño → Pacific Warming → Often Weak Indian Monsoon Association

119. La Niña
  • La Niña is abnormal cooling of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.
  • It often favours stronger Indian monsoon rainfall compared with El Niño conditions.
  • However, other atmospheric and oceanic factors also influence rainfall.
120. ENSO
  • ENSO stands for El Niño-Southern Oscillation.
  • It includes oceanic temperature changes and atmospheric pressure/circulation changes in the tropical Pacific.
📌 Must-Memorise

ENSO → El Niño + La Niña + Southern Oscillation

121. Southern Oscillation
  • Southern Oscillation refers to large-scale changes in atmospheric pressure between the western and eastern tropical Pacific.
  • It is linked with El Niño and La Niña.
122. Southern Oscillation Index
  • SOI is an atmospheric-pressure-based indicator used to monitor ENSO conditions.
  • It is associated with pressure differences across the tropical Pacific.
123. Indian Ocean Dipole
  • Indian Ocean Dipole is a pattern of sea-surface temperature differences between western and eastern equatorial Indian Ocean regions.
  • Positive and negative phases can influence Indian monsoon rainfall.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

IOD → Indian Ocean Temperature Contrast

124. Positive IOD
  • In a positive IOD, western equatorial Indian Ocean waters are relatively warmer than waters near Indonesia.
  • Positive IOD conditions can sometimes support Indian monsoon rainfall.
125. Negative IOD
  • In a negative IOD, eastern equatorial Indian Ocean waters near Indonesia are relatively warmer.
  • Such conditions can alter monsoon circulation differently.
126. Monsoon Is Multi-Factorial

Indian monsoon strength depends on interactions among:

  • Land-sea temperature contrast.
  • ENSO.
  • Indian Ocean Dipole.
  • Snow conditions.
  • Jet streams.
  • Monsoon depressions.
  • Intra-seasonal circulation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Indian monsoon cannot be explained by only one factor.

127. Monsoon Onset vs Monsoon Amount
  • Early onset does not automatically mean above-normal seasonal rainfall.
  • Late onset does not automatically mean drought.
  • Total rainfall depends on the entire season.
128. Rainfall Variability
  • Low-rainfall areas generally show greater year-to-year variability.
  • Rajasthan is therefore more drought-prone than very wet areas of the northeast.
129. Coefficient of Variation — Concept
  • Rainfall variability may be expressed statistically using measures such as coefficient of variation.
  • Higher variability means rainfall is less reliable from year to year.
130. Cyclones and Indian Climate
  • Tropical cyclones form over warm ocean waters.
  • Bay of Bengal historically produces many cyclones affecting India's eastern coast.
  • Arabian Sea cyclones can affect the western coast.
  • Cyclones contribute substantial short-duration rainfall.
131. Bay of Bengal Cyclones

Most vulnerable coastal regions include:

  • West Bengal.
  • Odisha.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Tamil Nadu.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bay Cyclones → East Coast

132. Tamil Nadu Cyclone Season
  • Tamil Nadu is particularly vulnerable during October-December.
  • This overlaps with northeast monsoon season.
  • Cyclones and depressions can provide large amounts of seasonal rainfall.
133. Coastal vs Interior Rainfall Mechanisms

Coastal rainfall is influenced by:

  • Moist maritime winds.
  • Cyclones.
  • Orographic effects near coastal mountains.

Interior rainfall depends more on:

  • Monsoon depressions.
  • Convection.
  • Distance from moisture source.
  • Relief.
134. Convectional Rainfall
  • Strong surface heating causes warm air to rise.
  • Rising air cools and condenses.
  • Short-duration heavy showers and thunderstorms can result.
  • Pre-monsoon storms often have a convective component.
135. Cyclonic Rainfall
  • Cyclonic rainfall occurs due to uplift around low-pressure systems, depressions and cyclones.
  • It can extend over large areas.
  • Tropical cyclones are important for Tamil Nadu's northeast monsoon rainfall.
136. Orographic vs Convectional vs Cyclonic Rainfall

Orographic:

  • Mountain uplift.

Convectional:

  • Surface heating.

Cyclonic:

  • Low-pressure system uplift.
📌 Must-Memorise

Three Main Rainfall Mechanisms → Orographic + Convectional + Cyclonic

137. Tamil Nadu Climatic Regions — Broad Pattern

Tamil Nadu contains:

  • Humid western mountain zones.
  • Semi-arid interior regions.
  • Tropical coastal plains.
  • Southern districts influenced by both monsoons.
138. Western Tamil Nadu
  • Western mountain slopes receive significant southwest monsoon rainfall.
  • Areas east of the Western Ghats receive much less because of rain-shadow effects.
  • Local elevation produces cooler conditions in the Nilgiris.
139. Eastern Tamil Nadu
  • Eastern coastal districts depend heavily on northeast monsoon rainfall.
  • Cyclonic systems from the Bay of Bengal can produce intense rainfall.
  • Rainfall variability creates drought and flood risk.
140. Tamil Nadu Seasonal Importance

For Tamil Nadu:

  • June-September → Southwest monsoon influence, especially west.
  • October-December → Northeast monsoon, especially east and coastal districts.
  • January-February → Relatively dry/cool.
  • March-May → Hot weather season.
141. Climate and Natural Vegetation
  • Heavy-rainfall areas support dense forests.
  • Moderate-rainfall areas support deciduous forests.
  • Low-rainfall areas support thorn and scrub vegetation.
  • Altitude creates mountain vegetation zones.
142. Climate and Soils

Climate affects:

  • Weathering.
  • Leaching.
  • Organic matter decomposition.
  • Soil moisture.
  • Erosion.

Thus climate influences soil development.

143. Climate and Settlement
  • Extreme deserts and high mountains support sparse populations.
  • Moderate plains and coastal climates support dense settlement.
  • Water availability strongly affects population concentration.
144. Important Climate Instruments — Link

Common meteorological instruments include:

  • Thermometer → Temperature.
  • Barometer → Atmospheric pressure.
  • Rain gauge → Rainfall.
  • Hygrometer → Humidity.
  • Anemometer → Wind speed.
  • Wind vane → Wind direction.
📌 TNPSC Favourite

Instrument ↔ Measurement

145. Rain Gauge
  • Rainfall is measured using a rain gauge.
  • Rainfall is generally expressed in millimetres.
146. Barometer
  • Atmospheric pressure is measured by a barometer.
  • Pressure is commonly expressed in hectopascals in meteorology.
147. Anemometer
  • An anemometer measures wind speed.
148. Wind Vane
  • Wind vane shows wind direction.
  • Wind direction is named for the direction from which the wind originates.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Northeast wind → Comes from northeast.

149. Hygrometer
  • Hygrometer measures humidity.
150. Climograph
  • A climograph combines temperature and precipitation information for a location.
  • It helps compare seasonal climate patterns.
151. Major Climatic Contrasts in India

Examples:

  • Mawsynram → Extremely wet.
  • Jaisalmer → Arid.
  • Ladakh → Cold desert.
  • Mumbai → Maritime.
  • Delhi → Continental.
  • Chennai → Northeast-monsoon-dominated coastal climate.
  • Ooty → Cool highland.
152. Monsoon and Western Ghats — Map Fact

Windward side:

  • Konkan.
  • Goa.
  • Coastal Karnataka.
  • Kerala.

Leeward side:

  • Interior Maharashtra.
  • Karnataka Plateau.
  • Parts of Tamil Nadu.
153. Monsoon and Northeast India — Map Fact

Very high rainfall occurs in:

  • Meghalaya.
  • Assam.
  • Arunachal Pradesh.
  • Himalayan foothill regions.
154. Rainfall and Rajasthan
  • Rainfall generally decreases westward in Rajasthan.
  • Western desert areas receive very little rainfall.
  • Eastern Rajasthan receives more because it is closer to monsoon pathways.
155. Winter Rain and Himalayas
  • Western disturbances produce snowfall over Jammu-Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand highlands.
  • This snow contributes to river flow during warmer months.
156. Climate Change Link
  • Long-term climate change can modify temperature, rainfall intensity, heat waves, glacier behaviour and sea-level conditions.
  • Detailed climate-change facts will be covered separately in Chapter 26.
